endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Patient & Family Advisory Council (PFAC) or Community Advisory Body AI incidents or material changes affecting the broader patient population, access, or community trust; periodic AI governance updates regardless of incident status; pre-deployment, pilot, and sunset decisions for higher risk AI solutions.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether informing patient and community advisory bodies about higher-risk AI decisions, incidents, and governance updates preserves community trust, and no supplied study documents the trust hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI, which describes the practice without reporting outcome data.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. A framework that describes a practice is expert opinion, and it cannot be graded for effect. Certainty about whether advisory-body reporting changes trust, engagement, or incident response therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The only endorsing source is the CHAI governance playbook, which is a voluntary framework. It lists advisory councils as recipients of incident reports, material changes, periodic updates, and pre-deployment, pilot, and sunset decisions for higher-risk tools. The supplied material cites no statute or regulation that requires this reporting, so adoption would rest on institutional policy.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems that report AI deployment, pilot, sunset, and incident decisions to patient and community advisory bodies with systems that do not. Useful outcomes would include measured patient and community trust, advisory-body influence on deployment or sunset decisions, and time from incident to public disclosure. The hazard itself, loss of trust when AI decisions go unshared, also lacks documentation in the supplied evidence.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Nothing in the supplied evidence shows whether advisory bodies represent these groups or whether reports reach them in usable languages and reading levels. Systems that adopt the practice may need to check advisory-body membership and report formats on their own, because the evidence offers no guidance.
